When Everything Feels Heavy

Upper School · Counselor-led small group, 25 minutes (one-on-one version below) · Any grade

Download PowerPoint Arrow keys or a clicker to move · N shows your notes · F for full screen · Esc to stop

Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Say what stays in the room and what you’d have to act on. Keep the group on the material, never on personal disclosures, and follow up one on one with anyone who seems to be carrying more.

Every student in the room

On the tell-one-adult step, say that families talk about mental health differently, and that a student can start with sleep, energy or stress if their family doesn't use the word depression.

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 6 · Notes

Ask: “Why might depression in teens look like anger more than tears?” Doctors count an irritable mood as a core sign under 18. Looking okay and being okay aren’t the same.

Slide 7 · Notes

Forbes et al. (2009): teens with depression showed less reward response to winning. The amygdala reacts more to sad or threatening cues; planning gets less bandwidth. These are group patterns; no scan diagnoses one person.

Thumbs up, down, or flat hand, then the answer.

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 10 · Notes

Gould et al. (2005). The most at-risk students seemed less distressed after being asked.

Slide 11 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 12 · Notes

Weed comes up; keep it factual. Gobbi pooled 11 long-term studies.

Slide 13 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 14 · Notes

TADS (March et al., 2007) found most teens responded by 36 weeks, highest with combined treatment.

Slide 15 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 16 · Notes

Two minutes in pairs. Keep it general.

Slide 17 · Notes

Take a few. Then: run the loop the other way.

Slide 18 · Notes

Behavioral activation runs the loop the other way: schedule small things first. Ekers’ review of 26 trials found a solid, moderate benefit. Noetel’s 218 trials: walking, yoga and strength training helped.

Slide 19 · Notes

Ask: “Which of these is the smallest step you could take this week?” Add a fifth: count small wins, one line a day, because depression erases them.

Slide 20 · Notes

Keep it about Sophie. A friend’s small invite and an adult who knows can both help.

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 22 · Notes

Irritability counts. If a friend ever talks about not wanting to be here, that’s a now: an adult or 988.

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Students write it now and keep it. If a family doesn’t use the word depression, a student can start with sleep, energy or stress.

Close: “If you or a friend ever has thoughts of dying, call or text 988 or come find me. If anything today hit close to home, I’d like to check in with you this week.”

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students learn how depression differs from a bad week, why it often looks like irritability in teens, why waiting to feel like it keeps people stuck, and leave with a small menu of actions for hard days and one adult they could tell.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • Index cards, one per student
  • Pens
  • The take-home link to share afterward

Flow

  1. 3 minBefore we start, and the volume turned down (private checks)
  2. 3 minHow common, and sad or depression?
  3. 4 minWhat depression changes in the brain
  4. 5 minMyth or real? One per slide
  5. 3 minTurn and talk, share out
  6. 3 minThe loop, and action first
  7. 4 minSophie and Theo, your hard-day menu, close

One on one (about 15 minutes)

One on one: start with the volume-down list and let the student point to what fits (3). Sad or depression, framed around what they've noticed (3). The downward spiral and action first (4). Build the hard-day menu together, and name one adult at home or school who should know (5).

Before you teach
Who's in the group.

This works best with students who are struggling but not in acute crisis. A student with active suicidal thinking needs an individual risk assessment first, not a group.

Keep it about the material.

Group members will be at different places. Let them talk about the ideas and the invented scenarios; save personal history for individual time so nobody overshares in front of peers.

Name the limits of confidentiality.

Say up front what stays in the room and what you'd have to act on. Students talk more freely when the rules are clear.

Irritability counts.

Some students, often boys, won't recognize themselves in "sad." Lead with irritability, flatness and "I don't care" so they see themselves in it.

Brain slides are group patterns.

No scan diagnoses one person. Present the brain material as a reason the struggle isn't laziness, not as proof of anything about a particular student.

Weed comes up.

Some students use cannabis to cope. Present the Gobbi finding as a link, not proof, and keep it curious rather than scolding so they keep talking.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Families talk about it differently.

In some families depression is a medical word; in others it's stress, nerves, tiredness, or something you pray about. Offer students words that fit their family, and name faith leaders as one possible adult.

Discrimination and loneliness are part of the load.

The causes list includes discrimination and bullying. Students of color, LGBTQ+ students and students with disabilities may be carrying that weight; name it without asking anyone to explain theirs.

Girls and boys show it differently.

The CDC numbers are higher for girls (53%). Boys more often show anger and withdrawal. Make sure both pictures are in the room.

LGBTQ+ students.

LGBTQ+ teens report higher rates of persistent sadness. Make sure examples and the "tell one adult" list include adults who will be safe for them.

Money and access.

Therapy and medication cost money and time. When you talk about treatment, mention school-based support and free lines so no student assumes help is out of reach.

Neurodivergence.

Depression in students with ADHD or autism can look like shutdown or more rigidity. Let students describe it in their own terms.

What the research says

40% of US high school students felt so sad or hopeless almost every day for two weeks or more that they stopped some usual activities; among girls it was 53%.

CDC, Youth Risk Behavior Survey, 2023

About 18% of 12- to 17-year-olds had a major depressive episode in the past year.

SAMHSA, National Survey on Drug Use and Health, 2023

In teens with depression, the striatum responded less when they won money, and the weaker the response, the less positive they felt in daily life.

Forbes et al., American Journal of Psychiatry, 2009

Pooling scans from nearly 9,000 people, the hippocampus was slightly smaller on average in people with repeated episodes or depression that began by 21; people in a first episode didn't differ.

Schmaal et al., Molecular Psychiatry, 2016

Pooling 11 long-term studies, teens who used cannabis had about 37% higher odds of depression as young adults, after accounting for earlier depression. A link, not proof of cause.

Gobbi et al., JAMA Psychiatry, 2019

A review of 26 trials found behavioral activation had a solid, moderate benefit over control groups.

Ekers et al., PLoS ONE, 2014

A review of 218 trials (mostly adults) found walking or jogging, yoga and strength training eased depression, more so at higher effort.

Noetel et al., BMJ, 2024

In 2,342 New York high school students randomly assigned to be asked about suicide or not, asking didn't raise distress or suicidal thinking. In a large trial, about 8 in 10 teens with depression responded after nine months of therapy, medicine or both.

Gould et al., JAMA, 2005 · March et al. (TADS), Archives of General Psychiatry, 2007
